summary: This memo defines a MIB for identifying the users associated with TCP connections, providing roughly the same function as the protocol in RFC 1413. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This is another way to ask which user owns a connection, using the network management system instead of a separate service. It is historic.

questions: snmp way to find the user of a tcp connection
how to identify tcp connection users with snmp
why is the ident mib historic
subtitle: Ask the network management system who owns a TCP connection.

tldr.problem: Administrators need to know which user owns a TCP connection to a server, similar to what the identification protocol provides, but integrated with network management.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB extends SNMP to add a table that maps TCP connections to the user running them on the destination host, including the operating system and character set of the response.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is historic; it was never widely adopted. The identification protocol (RFC 1413) remained the standard method, and modern systems prioritize security over exposure of user information.

today: RFC 1414 is Historic and was never widely deployed. The identification protocol (RFC 1413) remained the standard method for identifying TCP connection users, and modern networks tend to restrict exposure of user information for privacy and security reasons.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Identification MIB (RFC 1414) defines a Management Information Base for identifying users associated with TCP connections. It provides functionality similar to the identification protocol defined in RFC 1413, but works within the SNMP and network management framework rather than as a separate service.

End systems that support TCP may optionally implement this MIB. Administrators can query it to learn which user owns a given TCP connection on a managed host.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a set of questions you can ask a computer using network management. This MIB lets you ask "who is using this network connection?"

sections.title: The Identification Table
sections.content:
The MIB defines an identTable that contains one entry for each TCP connection on a host. Each entry includes:

  • identStatus: whether user information is available (noError) or not (unknownError)
  • identOpSys: the operating system type (0 to 40 octets), which also determines the format of the user ID and misc fields
  • identCharset: the character set (0 to 40 octets) used by the user ID and misc fields
  • identUserid: the user's identity (0 to 255 octets), interpreted based on the OS and charset
  • identMisc: miscellaneous information about the user (0 to 255 octets)

The table uses the TCP connection's local address, local port, remote address, and remote port as the key, allowing correlation with TCP connection statistics from MIB-II.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is like an address book for connections. For each connection, it says what system it came from, what language the name is in, who the user is, and any extra notes.

sections.title: Security Warnings
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes serious limitations on trusting this information:

Not authoritative: The information is only as trustworthy as the host providing it and the organization operating the host. A compromised system will return false information.

Privacy exposure: The MIB exposes information about users and processes, similar to a caller-ID service for networks. Organizations concerned with privacy should restrict access, just as they would restrict a finger server.

Not for access control: Using this information to make access-control decisions is strongly discouraged. It provides hints for auditing only, not proof.

Access to the MIB should be controlled via SNMP agent security mechanisms, and its use should be limited to auditing and normal network management functions.
sections.plainLanguage: The host might lie. Someone might trick it into saying a user is someone they are not. So you should never use this information to let someone into the system. It is just a hint for keeping records.

sections.title: Related Protocols
sections.content:
The MIB depends on several related standards and technologies:

  • RFC 1413 (Identification Protocol): the original identification service that this MIB emulates, using a dedicated TCP connection rather than SNMP
  • RFC 1155 (SMI): defines the structure and mechanisms for describing managed objects
  • RFC 1213 (MIB-II): the core set of management objects for TCP/IP networks, including TCP connection states
  • RFC 1157 (SNMP): the protocol used to query management objects

The RFC also references the ASSIGNED NUMBERS registry for valid operating system names and character sets.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB sits on top of SNMP, which is how computers ask each other questions about their health. It also uses the same connection table that tracks TCP connections.
